items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The language-switching trick (`#if 0` ... `""" #"` ... `" """` / `#endif`) has no comment explaining it, which the conventions ask for. The core logic uses single-letter names (`n`, `a, b`), which caps this at accept. Formatting is otherwise clean.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The file is 27 lines with one clear iterative implementation per language. There is no dead code and no debug output left behind. The only repetition is the one the polyglot format requires.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: C checks `if (argc < 2) return 1;` but exits silently, and `atoi(argv[1])` turns non-numeric input into 0 and prints it. Python has no argument check: `int(sys.argv[1])` raises an IndexError traceback, and negative n prints 0.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: Both versions are iterative and give f(0)=0 and f(1)=1. C uses `unsigned long long` and is correct up to n=93. Bad arguments are not rejected: in C, `atoi` turns "abc" into 0 and prints 0, and negative n prints 0 in both languages.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: It builds with plain `gcc` and also compiles cleanly under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic`, with no warnings after the fix in step [4]. Python runs without warnings. Each run prints only the number.
